source_metadata.title: Self-prompting and cross-model consensus enable reproducible data extraction from scientific literature with large language models

atoms.canonical_statement: The study evaluated four browser-based LLM workflows with progressively greater autonomy for extracting contextualized scientific data.
The fixed-corpus benchmark used seven frontier LLMs, 18 accessible primary articles, 39 experimental conditions, seven scored fields, and five independent runs per article.
The fixed-corpus benchmark retained supporting quotations, classified unmatched rows as extras, and used at least three positive runs for a majority-of-five result.
GPT-5.5 correctly reported 95.7% of expected values and experimental conditions under the expert prompt.

atoms.canonical_statement: The hardest articles required reasoning across methods, older terminology, conflicting constants, and OCR-corrupted exponents.
For self-authored prompts, each model produced three candidate prompts, aggregated them, and applied the master prompt five times to eight articles.
GPT-5.5's master prompt covered 88.2% of the expert prompt rubric.

atoms.canonical_statement: The organoid papers were hand selected to contain most guideline features, limiting external validity.
Browser products, hidden instructions, compute allocation, model versions, and interface behavior changed during the study.
Only one model flagged an included concept paper without being prompted, so source-type checks cannot be assumed.
Experts should define the question, corpus, and evidence standard; models should perform repeated extractions; and people should resolve disputed, contextual, or high-impact cases.
The repository provides prompts, raw outputs, curated data for all figures, and a tutorial for the fixed-corpus and self-prompting workflows.
